• Blue Origin New Shepard sounding rocket yields Lunar gravity by using centrifugal acceleration.
• These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.  
• A steady vehicle rotation of 11 RPM is established, with an effective radius of rotation of 1.22 m at the experiment location.  
• Two samples are burned simultaneously in air at normal pressure: Cotton-fiberglass composite fabric sheet and a 4-mm diameter 
rod of acrylic plastic (polymethyl methacrylate).  
• Flame images from two orthogonal cameras are used to determine flame spread and growth rates, and the burn lasts for over 
two and a half minutes.  
• The oxygen concentration in the chamber is measured.  As the burns progress, the oxygen concentration drops, enabling a 
limiting value for extinction to be defined.  
• The effect of Coriolis force is discussed.  
• Results from this experiment are compared to related 1-g work, drop tower tests, aircraft experiments, and modeling.  
• The results are applicable to NASA’s exploration efforts in that they guide the selection of fire-safe materials and environments 
and ensure safety of future spacecraft and Lunar habitats.  The data also provides fundamental understanding of fires.  
• Finally, the experiment is a steppingstone to the ultimate goal of performing burn tests on the Lunar surface in the Flammability 
of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment which is planned to launch in late 2026.

 History
• ZIN technologies brought on board October 2021
• Initial Planned launch was Spring 2023, Launch provider delay initially delayed launch into late Summer early Fall 2024, until 
it finally launched Feb 4 2025
• First mission sequence test was performed in July 2023
• Due to launch slip some improvements were made and last mission sequence test was ran in February 2024 before 
being shelved prior to flight. 
 Objectives
• Burn SIBAL fabric & PMMA 
• Conduct first-ever, long duration observation and measurement of flame spread in a partial-g environment
• Verify this platform is a viable means to obtain material flammability data in Lunar-g and will include an assessment of 
the Coriolis force on results
• Provide guidance for sample selection and test definition for a Lunar in-situ experiment
 Data
• First Flight
• Measurements of flame spread rate and output of other diagnostics, including g-level vs. time for the two samples
• Sample closeout photos and photos before and after each test
• Data from 1-g burns

levels close to those found on the moon. This was identified as a risk for the Human Landing 
System program. However, lunar gravity testing is largely limited to using a centrifuge in the

I. Introduction 
ASA has focused on material selection as a primary means of fire prevention.  The method for selecting fire safe 
materials has been NASA STD 6001 Test 1 (hereafter referred to as Test 1)1.  Test 1 is an upward flammability 
test that uses a consistent ignition source (known as the chemical igniter) that is considered to be a very strong ignition 
source1.  If the flame damaged zone is found to be less than 15.2 cm (6”), the material is determined to be self-
extinguishing for the test conditions. The concept was that with a strong ignition source in upward spread, the test will 
be conservative. The purpose of the test is not to identify materials that will never burn but rather to identify materials 
that do not burn easily and will self-extinguish in most situa tions. Given the test design, for most materials, Test 1 is 
an ignition test, if the material has enough specific heat or low enough heat release, it will pass but it might not pass 
with a bigger igniter or if the material were 
slightly preheated. In the case of thin materials 
of limited spread rate, it is possible for Test 1 to 
function as a flammability test.  
 Testing in drop towers and on reduced 
gravity aircraft 2,3 has shown that materials can 
have broader flammability limits (e.g. oxygen 
limits) at partial gravity levels close to those 
found on the moon and this was identified as a 
risk for the Human Landing System (HLS). 
Since our only repeatable access to lunar gravity 
is in the NASA GRC 5.2 second drop tower, 
using a centrifuge 3, testing has been limited to 
thinner materials that can be tested in 5.2 
seconds. This paper discusses the result of a test 
campaign to assess the change in material 
flammability at lunar gravity levels and to 
determine if there is a correction factor that could 
be applied to the results of NASA Test 1 to 
encompass lunar flammability limits.

low gravity spacecraft 4 demonstrate continuous 
ventilation in all open areas and there will be

rigorous analysis of the ignition of a solid in a hot boundary layer flow 7, 17. The boundary layer analysis is based on 
the novel and rigorous analysis by Niioka and co-workers 17 on the ignition of a solid fuel in a stagnation point flow. 
Both works successfully address the problem with similar co ncepts, basing the flame extinction problem in terms of 
heat transfer and chemical kinetics processes. 
Experimental Method 
The goal was to measure the change in the extinction limit between 1-g testing and lunar-g testing in the centrifuge.  
NASA Test 1 has a 15 cm (6 inch) burn criterion, so the test  time is much longer than the 5 seconds available in the 
drop tower.  Consequently a 5 second extinction criterion test program was developed to determine the change in the 
extinction limit in 1-g and lunar-g and apply this offset to NASA Test 1 flammability  limits for lunar material 
certification. The approach used in this test program was to conduct a study of concurrent-flow flammability-limits in

A. NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) Upward High-flow Oxygen Index Testing  
The WSTF testing was conducted using a WSTF 1.4 m3 (50 ft3) 
chamber that could provide continuous operation at 57 kPa. Installed 
in the chamber was a 7.4 cm ID by 30 cm long quartz tube duct (Fig 
5) where the 5.2 cm by 14.0 cm samples were tested. This system was 
based on the HOI ISO Standard.18 Below the test section was a flow 
conditioning section above an inlet plenum. The flow was supplied 
by a mass flow system which established the desired oxygen 
concentration and flow rate. The sample material was sandwiched 
between two, u-shaped, thin stainless-steel plates with the open end 
oriented downwards towards the igniter. The igniter was a retractable 
2.2 mm OD ceramic rod that swung away from the sample after 
ignition. The ceramic rod was heated by 0.29 mm Kanthal-A wire 
woven through the 4 holes in the ceramic.  The front and the back of 
the sample were recorded by video cameras. After installation in the 
flow duct, and pressure was established in the chamber, the sample 
was exposed to a 10 cm/s primer  flow at the target oxygen 
concentration. The igniter was activated until the sample was ignited. 
The igniter was retracted, and the flame was allowed to establish for 
1 second before the flow was increased to the test condition at the 
same oxygen concentration. The flow increase occurs in 
approximately a second. If the flame extinguished in 5 seconds, it was

B. NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) Partial Gravity Testing   
The GRC testing was conducted using the centrifuge test facility in the ZGRF 5.2 second drop tower (Fig. 6).3 The 
chamber is 299 l in volume with an I.D. of 81.2 cm and an internal height if 30.5 cm. To achieve lunar gravity, the 
chamber was rotated at 20.4 RPM for several minutes before the drop (I.e. onset of microgravity) to bring the air in 
the chamber to near solid body rotation. In this configur ation, (during the drop) the gravity vector was radially 
outwards, and the resulting buoyant flow was radially inward  To achieve upward spread the long axis of the sample 
is oriented radially and ignited on the outside edge so th e resulting buoyant flow is conc urrent with the direction of 
flame spread. Owing to the short radius of rotation, ther e was a significant gravity gradient. The flames, however, 
(especially when near the extinction limits) did not spread  significantly during the drop, so the g-variation was 
considered to have a minimal impact on the results. The short radius of rotation also caused a significant Coriolis force 
in the tangential direction19. Initial tests found that the effect was mitigated by orienting the sample surface parallel to 
the axis of rotation (long edge down) so the Coriolis fl ow was impeded by the sample surface. The igniter was a 
ceramic igniter very similar to the one used at WSTF except it withdrew ver tically. To increase the number of tests 
for repeatability, two samples were ignite d and tested in each drop. The samples were several cm apart and offset 
vertically (Fig. 6) so they did not inte rfere with each other. The ignition region of the sample was exposed to a slow 
flow (~30 cm/s) of gas with an oxygen concentration 5 to 10% higher than the ambient. This enabled sample ignition 
in a chamber condition where the sample might be near the flammability limit. During the ignition interval, the drop 
rig is hanging at the top of the tower and is spinning to produce a 1/6 g radial acceleration in addition to the 1-g vertical 
force. This resulting buoyant flow prim arily directed laterally across the samp le is less successful at heating the 
unburned sample than the purely upward flow at WSTF. The drop tower operations require the system to operate 
autonomously so the entire process was controlled automatically by the drop rig. The ignition duration and the oxygen 
enhancement were varied based on experience with ignita bility of the material being tested. After a prescribed 
duration, the igniter is turned off and retracted. One seco nd later, the oxygen enhanced flow is turned off and the 
package is released. At this point, the flow is entirely driven by buoyancy. Since the bulk of the chamber is already at 
the target atmosphere, the buoyant flow immediately sweeps in the target conditions. Both samples were observed 
with separate front and edge view cameras. In post-test video analysis, if the sample was still burning at the end of the

III. Results and Discussion 
Five materials were tested in both facilities. The results are plotted with oxygen concentration versus force flow 
speed in figures 7-12. All materials were tested in the WSTF  facility for at least 4 flow rates (60, 80, 100, 144 cm/s) 
with PMMA having additional testing at 25 and 40 cm/s. Three of the materials typically fail NASA test 1 (are 
flammable) in air (PMMA, P213 Tape (fiberglass with an acrylic (PMMA) adhesive), and cotton t-shirt material) and 
two materials pass Test 1 in air  (polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro). The passed (o) and failed (x) tests are all shown 
on the plot. The limit (black circle) is the highest concentration where 5 (out  of 5) consecutive passes were observed. 
The horizontal axis is what could be measured in the labor atory, the forced flow veloci ty. Although estimates exist 
for the buoyant flow of spreading flames,16,20 near the extinction limit, the validity of these estimates is less clear, so 
the data are plotted with the forced velocity. The lunar gravity centrifuge data is shown with a horizontal line in the 
lower velocity range because the actual velocity (induced by the simulated gravity) is not known. The lunar-g limit

was also found by multiple passes (usually 4) below the lowe st oxygen concentration fail. In figures 7, 8 and 9, the 
lunar-g buoyant limit was found to be less than the extrap olated value (for any assumed buoyant velocity) from the 
WSTF testing. This result is contrary to expected behavior. The WSTF upward ignition is expected to heat the material 
more effectively thereby increasing the fuel concentrati on and increasing the Damköhler number seen in equation 8. 
The lower extinction concentration for the lunar-g testing for PMMA, P213 and flaming Beefy-T suggest that the 
buoyant velocity is very low, but it does not correlate with the WSTF data. Various differences in the test methods 
have been considered (turbulence at high flow rates, ignition times, delay after ignition before initiating the test, 
oxygen augmentation during ignition, and buoyancy-enhanced ignition heat transfer to the unburned fuel due to the 
sample orientation with respect to gravity) but have not been definitively found to be the cause. Further study of this 
unexplained behavior is warranted to before the UHOI can be accepted as a material flammability standard. Comparing

Lunar gravity has been found to increase the limits of flammability for some materials compared to Earth 
gravity, presenting a goldilocks zone of reduced convective heat loss, while generating enough buoyant 
flow to replenish fresh oxygen into the flame zone.  Combined with the elevated oxygen concentrations 
of planned Space Exploration Atmospheres (Sea), a long duration fire experiment in Lunar gravity is 
important to help understand and mitigate the increased risk.
Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) is a robotic, self-contained, combustion chamber which will 
be sent to the surface of the Moon on a Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) lander mission CP-21. 
The environmental control system can replicate and conduct fire experiments automatically in the 
expected atmospheres, specifically 21% oxygen at 14.7 psia, and 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia, which are of 
immediate interest to the Human Lander System (HLS) and Lunar Rover.
The laboratory prototype became operational this summer. There are four samples currently planned; 
two SIBAL fabrics (cotton/fiberglass blend) which will be burned in air and two acrylic rods which will be 
burned in Normoxic Space Exploration Atmospheres (SEA). One of each fuel will be burned upward and 
downward. SIBAL fabric has been found to only burn downward in air in lunar gravity (via Lunar gravity 
centrifuge and parabolic flight) where on Earth’s gravity it extinguishes immediately after ignition.

Conclusions
♦ We have made progress to address the exploration capability gaps identified by the SCLT
• Material flammability and flammability limits in Lunar-g is a high priority – especially because of the 
elevated %O2
♦ Owing to lack of access to partial gravity test platforms, the data set of lunar flammability 
tests is very small
♦ Theory and experimental results indicate that oxygen flammability limits in lunar-g are 
lower than those measured in 1-g
• The magnitude of ∆%O2 depends not only on the material but on the direction of burning (concurrent or 
opposed)
♦ The planned habitat atmosphere exacerbates these issues by enhancing the flammability
♦ Additional work is needed to establish a partial gravity flammability acceptance criterion
♦ Lunar gravity can change fire detection strategy depending on vehicle design
♦ Turning off forced air flow cannot be used as an extinguishment strategy
♦ Work on post-fire clean-up and emergency mask is progressing following an update to the 
sorbent packing procedure
